records.sourceFile: Heart rate variability in concussed college athletes - Follow-up study and biological sex differences.pdf

paper.citation: Doucet M, Brisebois H, McKerral M. Heart Rate Variability in Concussed College Athletes: Follow-Up Study and Biological Sex Differences. Brain Sciences. 2023;13:1669.
paper.abstract: Prospective longitudinal study of 169 college athletes (55 girls) with baseline HRV and symptom testing, followed through 30 concussions (8 girls) at 24 to 72 hours and at return to play. Baseline girls had higher sitting %VLF and more symptoms. After concussion, HRV showed no change in RMSSD, VLF or HF, and %HF showed a time by position by sex interaction, with girls higher at return to play.
paper.tldr: In 30 concussed college athletes followed from a preseason baseline, heart rate variability did not change over recovery overall, but the relative high-frequency measure followed different paths for boys and girls. With only 2 girls retested at return to play, this is a research signal, not a tool for clearing athletes.
paper.methods: Prospective longitudinal before-after cohort (STROBE) with baseline testing (symptom scales, anxiety and depression inventories, and 2 minutes each of standing and sitting HRV, required only for football and basketball) and retesting after concussion (T2, planned within 72 hours, mean 3.5 days excluding two athletes seen after more than a month) and before return to play (T3). Group differences were tested with t-tests and chi-square tests, and changes over time with mixed-model repeated-measures ANOVA with sex as a factor.
paper.findings: At baseline, girls had higher sitting %VLF (P = .001, large effect) and higher total symptom scores (P ≤ .001) than boys. In the concussed group, RMSSD, VLF and HF showed no significant time or sex effect, while the time by position by sex interaction for %HF was significant (P = .022), with higher sitting %HF in girls at T3 (based on 2 girls). Average return to play was 20.3 days (SD 14.0) and did not differ by sex.
paper.limitations: The concussed sample is small and the girls' HRV data are very sparse (1 girl at T1, 2 at T3), so sex-specific results are unstable. No control group was retested at season end because of COVID-19 school closures, and sleep and menstrual cycle were not measured. The text reports the sex effect as a 39% difference at T3, the boys' within-group changes are described but not tested, and one correlation (affective symptoms with prior concussion, r = 0.031, P = .031) is internally inconsistent. The first post-concussion test fell outside the planned 72-hour window for many athletes (mean 3.5 days, and two after more than a month).
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not use HRV to detect a concussion or to clear an athlete for play, which the authors state the study does not support. If HRV is collected, record biological sex and interpret sex-specific patterns with caution. Clinical symptom monitoring should continue to give extra attention to vestibular-somatic symptoms, the only symptom class that returned to baseline by return to play.
paper.athleteDev: Not directly applicable to performance. The study looked at autonomic recovery after concussion and did not link HRV to training load, readiness or performance outcomes, so these values should not guide training decisions.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return to play after concussion, but the study cannot be used to clear an athlete. HRV did not show a clear time pattern across the group, and the sex-specific %HF finding rests on very few girls at return to play, so no sex-specific return threshold can be set from it.

records.sourceFile: Short term effects of two different recovery strategies on muscle contractile properties in healthy active men - A randomised cross-over study.pdf

paper.citation: Mur-Gimeno E, Sebio-Garcia R, Solé J, Lleida A, Moras G. Short-term effects of two different recovery strategies on muscle contractile properties in healthy active men: a randomised cross-over study. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022;40(6):646-654.
paper.abstract: Randomised cross-over study of 28 healthy active men who performed a fatigue protocol of the knee extensors and then received hot-water immersion, cold-water immersion or passive rest. Tensiomyography of the vastus medialis was recorded up to one hour. Relativised displacement and velocity of deformation rose more after hot-water immersion than after cold-water immersion, and hot-water immersion was no better than passive rest for displacement.
paper.tldr: In a small crossover study of active men, 15 minutes of hot-water immersion after fatiguing exercise produced faster changes in muscle contractile properties than cold-water immersion over the first 45 minutes. These are short-term changes in muscle measures, not proof of better recovery or performance.
paper.methods: Randomised cross-over study with three recovery conditions (hot-water immersion at 42 degrees C, cold-water immersion at 10 degrees C, passive rest) for 15 minutes after a fatigue protocol of five sets of eight repetitions at 8RM, separated by one-week washouts. Tensiomyography measured maximal displacement and contraction time of the vastus medialis before, after the fatigue and recovery, and at 15, 30, 45 and 60 minutes. Displacement and velocity of deformation were relativised to muscle size and analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: Hot-water immersion gave a larger relativised displacement than cold-water immersion immediately after recovery (mean difference +4.02 mm, 95% CI 0.75 to 7.3, P = .001), but no difference from passive rest. Relativised velocity of deformation was higher after hot than cold immersion immediately (P < .0001), at 15 minutes (P = .001) and at 45 minutes (P = .004). Against passive rest, hot immersion was higher only at 45 minutes (P = .008), and cold immersion was lower at 15 minutes (P = .005).
paper.limitations: Only 28 men were studied, all described as healthy and active rather than as athletes, and only one muscle was measured. Although the design was cross-over, the analysis treated condition as a between-subject factor (F(2,81)), intramuscular temperature was not recorded, the assessor was not blinded, and no post-recovery performance test was included. Baseline displacement was already higher before hot immersion, and the conclusion that velocity was enhanced versus passive rest immediately and at 15 minutes is not supported by the reported P values (.015 against a threshold of P < .01).
paper.practicalImplications: For active men after a fatiguing lower-body session, hot-water immersion appears to avoid the short-term drop in muscle contractile measures seen after cold-water immersion. The study did not test performance, soreness or women, so it cannot show that hot immersion improves recovery or should replace cold immersion.
paper.athleteDev: Limited direct performance application. The study measured short-term muscle contractile properties, not strength, power or sport performance, so it can suggest a recovery option to test with athletes but cannot show training benefit.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study used healthy men after an induced fatigue protocol, with no injured participants and no return-to-play measures.

records.sourceFile: Effects of external counterpulsation on post-exercise recovery in elite rugby league players.pdf

paper.citation: Roberts LA, Caia J, James LP, Scott TJ, Kelly VG. Effects of external counterpulsation on post-exercise recovery in elite rugby league players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019.
paper.abstract: Seven elite National Rugby League players completed two identical 60-minute field conditioning sessions 48 hours apart, each followed by 30 minutes of external counterpulsation or a placebo. Cycling peak power and accumulated peak power rose after counterpulsation, the testosterone to cortisol ratio was higher at 5 hours, and IL-1ra rose after counterpulsation.
paper.tldr: In seven elite rugby league players, a single 30-minute session of external counterpulsation after a pre-season conditioning session was followed by higher short-term cycling power and some hormonal changes than placebo. This is a small proof-of-concept study, and the claims of reduced inflammation and better performance go beyond what the data show.
paper.methods: Randomised, placebo-controlled crossover with two endurance-focused field conditioning sessions 48 hours apart, each followed by 30 minutes of external counterpulsation or an identical placebo with no pressure. Five 20-second cycling sprints, saliva and blood samples, and perceptions were collected before, after and 5 hours post-exercise. Outcomes were analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc tests and P ≤ .05.
paper.findings: Peak power (+11%, P = .028) and accumulated peak power (+14%, P = .027) increased after counterpulsation with no change after placebo, while other power measures did not change. The plasma testosterone to cortisol ratio showed a condition by time interaction (P = .015) and was above baseline and placebo after counterpulsation (P = .017 to .029). IL-1ra rose further from post-exercise to 5 hours after counterpulsation (P = .024), and the salivary alpha-amylase to IgA ratio fell after counterpulsation (P = .013), although that ratio showed no condition or interaction effect.
paper.limitations: Only 7 players were studied, plasma results came from 6, and many outcomes were tested at P ≤ .05 with no correction. The power comparison with placebo rests on a time effect rather than a reported interaction test, and the methods list countermovement jump outcomes that the results do not report. The placebo applied no pressure and comfort ratings differed sharply (8.7 placebo vs 1.4 counterpulsation), so blinding was unlikely to hold; baseline blood pressure already differed between conditions, the abstract says inflammation fell although IL-1ra rose, and the device manufacturer funded the grant.
paper.practicalImplications: In pre-season rugby league, staff could consider external counterpulsation as one option when two sessions fall on the same day, but it should be tested with more players and in game-like settings first. The study does not show that it reduces inflammation or improves match performance, and it used one familiarisation session.
paper.athleteDev: Relevant to performance between sessions. A single session was followed by higher short-term peak cycling power in seven players, but the conditioning session was not game-like, and no sport-specific performance was tested.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study used healthy-screened elite players after a conditioning session and included no injured athletes and no return-to-play measures.

records.sourceFile: Heavy Hitters, Light Sleepers - Collision Frequency and Locomotor Load on Sleep Architecture in Professional Rugby Union Players.pdf

paper.citation: Uchiyama K, Peeling P, Halson SL, Reid M, Wallman K, Walsh J, et al. Heavy hitters, light sleepers: collision frequency and locomotor load on sleep architecture in professional rugby union players. European Journal of Sport Science. 2025;25(9):e70052.
paper.abstract: Retrospective study of 13 professional male rugby union players across three matches, using a home-based wearable sleep device, video-coded collisions and GPS load in a linear mixed-effects model. Each collision was associated with less total sleep and less REM sleep, while total distance was associated with more REM sleep and high-speed distance with less.
paper.tldr: After professional rugby union matches, players who made more collisions slept less and got less REM sleep that night, while higher running distance was linked to more REM sleep. This is a small retrospective study of match nights only, so use it to plan individual post-match sleep support, not as proof of cause.
paper.methods: Retrospective observational study of male professional players named in the matchday squad for three 2023 Super Rugby matches. Post-match sleep was recorded with a forehead wearable (Somfit) and scored in 30-second epochs by one scorer, while collisions came from Opta event data and running and acceleration metrics from 10 Hz GPS units. Linear mixed-effects models included player as a random intercept.
paper.findings: Each additional collision was associated with about 4 minutes less total sleep (P = .006) and about 2 minutes less REM sleep (P < .001), and REM proportion fell by 0.6% (P = .021). Each extra 500 m of total distance was associated with 6 minutes more REM sleep (P = .014), and each extra 100 m of high-speed distance with 7 minutes less (P = .020). Home matches were linked to later sleep onset and offset (about 1.9 hours each, P = .037 and .011); kick-off time had no effect.
paper.limitations: The sample is 13 players and 20 nights, with no non-match or baseline sleep for comparison, and the wearable is a forehead EEG device validated at 63 to 79% agreement with polysomnography rather than laboratory PSG. Many sleep and demand variables were tested without multiplicity correction, caffeine, alcohol and sleep disorders were not controlled, and the only home match was also the only evening kick-off, so location, travel and time zone cannot be separated. Collision counts also track minutes played (starters averaged 21 collisions, finishers 10), and the study did not measure next-day function.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could track sleep after high-contact matches and consider individual post-match sleep plans for players with heavy collision loads, as the authors suggest. Because the study did not test any sleep intervention, it cannot show which plan works, and high-speed running may also be worth monitoring given its link to less REM sleep.
paper.athleteDev: Indirect relevance to performance. Less sleep and REM sleep after heavy-collision matches may affect next-day function, which the study did not measure, but it can inform individual recovery planning after matches.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study examined squad players after matches and did not include injured players or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Immediate Effects of Overnight Long-Haul Travel on Physical and Cognitive Performance and Sleep in Professional Male Rugby Union Players (a 2-Part Study).pdf

paper.citation: Uchiyama K, Peeling P, Halson SL, Reid M, Wallman K, Walsh J, et al. Immediate Effects of Overnight Long-Haul Travel on Physical and Cognitive Performance and Sleep in Professional Male Rugby Union Players (a 2-Part Study). International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2025 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Overnight long-haul travel reduced sleep during the trip in professional rugby union players. After travel with minimal time-zone change (Part I, +1 time zone), drop-jump reactive strength index was below baseline on the first and third mornings after arrival, while in a separate trip (Part II, -6 time zones) psychomotor vigilance was slowed in flight and back near baseline by the first morning after arrival. The authors recommend arriving more than 3 days before matches.
paper.tldr: A long overnight flight cut sleep by several hours and left reactive jump strength down for about 3 days after arrival in professional rugby players. Thinking and reaction speed were slowed during the flight but were back near normal the morning after the first night at the destination.
paper.methods: Prospective observational study with 43 professional male rugby players on two overseas trips. Part I (n = 24, Perth to Tokyo, +1 time zone) measured drop-jump and multirebound-jump performance on five mornings. Part II (n = 24, Perth to Johannesburg, -6 time zones) measured psychomotor vigilance and visual analog fatigue scales at home, in flight and on arrival. Wrist actigraphy with sleep diaries tracked sleep, and linear mixed-effects models with player as a random intercept were used.
paper.findings: In both parts, total sleep fell during travel compared with home (Part I -219 min, Part II -334 min, both P < .001); sleep on the first arrival night was not significantly different from home (Part I 490 vs 421 min). In Part I, drop-jump RSI was lower than home on arrival day 1 (-8%, P = .002) and day 3 (-12%, P < .001), drop-jump flight time was lower on all 3 arrival mornings, and multirebound-jump flight time was reduced on day 1. In Part II, mean reaction time for responses at or under 500 ms was slower in flight (+8%, P < .001) and mental fatigue rose during travel (+12 on the visual analog scale, P = .017); on the morning after arrival reaction time was back near baseline and mental fatigue was lower than at home.
paper.limitations: The two trips differed in direction, duration and time-zone shift, so the authors state the results cannot be interpreted together. Sample sizes were 24 per part and some data were missing (79% of jump, 69% of PVT and 86% of perceptual data collected). Part II home testing was in the afternoon after training and arrival testing in the morning, which may explain the better arrival scores. Recovery was not measured after day 3, and the abstract reports a -7% day 1 drop-jump RSI change while the results report -8%.
paper.practicalImplications: Long overnight flights reduce sleep and can leave lower-limb explosive ability reduced for about 3 days after arrival in this group. Teams planning long trips with limited time before competition should consider arriving earlier and scheduling cognitively demanding meetings in the morning after the first night at the destination. Sleep, compression and hydration strategies are proposed by the authors but were not shown to work in this study.
paper.athleteDev: Long overnight travel on a route with little time-zone change (Part I) left drop-jump reactive strength down for 3 mornings after arrival, so the authors suggest arriving more than 3 days before a match. Cognitive tasks may be placed in the morning after arrival, as reaction speed had recovered by then.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It involved players travelling for competition and did not measure injured athletes, rehabilitation progress or injury risk.

records.sourceFile: Monitoring collegiate soccer players during a congested match schedule- Heart rate variability versus subjective wellness measures.pdf

paper.citation: Rabbani A, Karami Baseri M, Reisi J, Clemente FM, Kargarfard M. Monitoring collegiate soccer players during a congested match schedule: Heart rate variability versus subjective wellness measures. Physiology & Behavior. 2018;194:527-531.
paper.abstract: Eight collegiate soccer players were tracked across a low-load training phase and a high-load congested match phase. Session RPE and the Hooper wellness index rose substantially during the match phase, while heart rate variability (Ln rMSSD and SDNN) changed only trivially. Changes in wellness scores tracked changes in session RPE closely, and changes in heart rate variability did not.
paper.tldr: In a small group of collegiate soccer players, a congested match schedule clearly worsened self-rated sleep, stress, fatigue and soreness, but a single morning heart rate variability reading barely changed. Subjective wellness questionnaires tracked training load better than single time point heart rate variability in this study.
paper.methods: Within-group study of eight collegiate soccer players (21.1 +/- 3.4 years) over two weeks of spring training. A low-load phase of four training sessions was compared with a high-load phase of four congested matches. Morning Hooper wellness index and subsets were recorded with a 7-point questionnaire, and supine Ln rMSSD and SDNN were recorded for one minute on a smartphone app with a chest strap. Session RPE x duration was used for internal load. Standardized differences (Cohen's d) and Pearson correlations between changes in session RPE and changes in each measure were calculated.
paper.findings: Mean session RPE rose from 287.5 to 569.4 AU (+108.9%, effect size 1.35) and accumulated session RPE rose by +148.4% (effect size 2.16). The Hooper index increased by +49.8% (effect size 1.05), with sleep, stress, fatigue and soreness all increasing (effect sizes 0.68 to 1.06). Ln rMSSD changed by -2.1% and SDNN by +8.2%, both trivial (effect size -0.15 and 0.15). Changes in the Hooper index were strongly correlated with changes in session RPE (r = 0.72), while changes in Ln rMSSD were not (r = 0.10).
paper.limitations: Only eight players were studied, from one collegiate team and a single tournament, and the sex of the players is not stated. Heart rate variability was measured on one morning per phase rather than as a rolling average, which the authors note is the recommended approach, so the heart rate variability result may understate its use. External load was not measured, and the correlations rest on very small numbers, with wide confidence intervals for several of them. The authors state that a longer observation period and a professional sample are needed.
paper.practicalImplications: When only one measurement time point is available after a congested match block, the Hooper wellness questionnaire moved with training load while a single heart rate variability reading did not. Staff could favor a brief wellness questionnaire for this kind of snapshot check. The study does not show how heart rate variability performs when averaged over several days.
paper.athleteDev: After a four-match congested tournament phase in collegiate soccer, the Hooper wellness index rose by about half while heart rate variability barely changed. A short wellness questionnaire may be the more sensitive single snapshot of accumulated fatigue when deciding on load or line-ups during congested fixtures.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It involved collegiate players in a training and tournament setting and did not assess injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Evaluating methods for imputing missing data from longitudinal monitoring of athlete workload.pdf

paper.citation: Benson LC, Stilling C, Owoeye OBA, Emery CA. Evaluating Methods for Imputing Missing Data from Longitudinal Monitoring of Athlete Workload. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2021;20:188-196.
paper.abstract: Ten methods for filling in missing jump count and RPE workload data were compared in a season of youth basketball. The best single method was the team mean for the session with the missing value, and the best overall was a team machine learning model. Season-level jump counts and sRPE remained strongly correlated after multiple imputation.
paper.tldr: When workload data are missing in youth basketball, filling a gap with the team's average for that same session was the most accurate simple option. Models that also use each player's own history were more accurate still but require more data and software.
paper.methods: Secondary analysis of jump counts (per hour, from a wearable jump counter) and RPE from 93 high school basketball players across eight teams in one season. Known values were removed at random (1% at a time) and ten imputation methods were scored by root mean squared error, using a generalized estimating equation. The best-performing methods were then used for multiple imputation of the real missing data, and season jump count was correlated with season sRPE.
paper.findings: The team machine learning model had the lowest error (8.5 jumps/hour and 1.1 RPE points using all sessions) and was significantly better than all other methods. The team mean for the same session (11.7 jumps/hour, 1.4 RPE points) and the individual machine learning model (12.2 jumps/hour, 1.4 RPE points) were next best. Using only game or only practice sessions to impute did not reduce error. Season jump count and season sRPE were strongly correlated in the original data (r = 0.74) and after multiple imputation (pooled r = 0.79), and imputation raised mean season totals (jumps 740 to 866; sRPE 11,268 to 14,289 AU).
paper.limitations: Data came from one season, eight teams and one jump-counting device, and partial-participation sessions were excluded. Errors were tested by removing 1% of known values at a time from datasets that already had 7.7% to 49.4% effective missingness, while real missingness reached 93% of full-participation sessions for some teams. The data were not missing completely at random, team-based methods cannot be calculated when a whole team is missing a measure, and non-workload variables such as position and injury status were not used.
paper.practicalImplications: For single gaps in youth basketball workload, using the same-session team mean is a reasonable and simple choice. Multiple imputation with several predictors is better suited to season-long totals, but needs validated software and enough data to train a model. Imputed values should be reported as estimates, not as measured workload.
paper.athleteDev: For youth basketball workload records, a same-session team mean is the most accurate simple way to fill a single missing jump count or RPE value. Season totals built from imputed data should be interpreted as estimates.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It analysed workload data in high school players and did not assess injured athletes or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Symptoms of Overtraining in Resistance Exercise - International Cross-Sectional Survey.pdf

paper.citation: Grandou C, Wallace L, Coutts AJ, Bell L, Impellizzeri FM. Symptoms of Overtraining in Resistance Exercise: International Cross-Sectional Survey. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: In a survey of 605 competitive resistance-based athletes, most reported a past unexplained performance decline, usually lasting 1 week to 1 month. General fatigue was the most common symptom at every duration, and most cases also involved non-training stressors. The authors conclude that no single symptom profile can distinguish the stages of overtraining.
paper.tldr: Among competitive strength and power athletes who had an unexplained drop in performance, general fatigue was the most common symptom and most cases had other stressors outside training. No single symptom reliably signalled overtraining, so staff should watch a combination of performance and symptoms.
paper.methods: Anonymous 46-item online survey (REDCap) distributed through industry contacts and social media in July and August 2019 to competitive athletes in resistance-based sports, with 605 eligible responses from 760 completions. Athletes who had never had an unexplained performance decline stopped at section 3. Frequencies were calculated by sport, and chi-square tests examined links between maladaptation and training history or style.
paper.findings: 70.9% of respondents reported a past unexplained decrease in performance. Duration was under 1 week in 26.8%, 1 week to 1 month in 43.8%, 1 to 3 months in 13.1% and over 4 months in 4.7%. General fatigue was the most common symptom overall (35.7%) and in every duration group, and musculoskeletal aches and pain were the second most common in acute cases. 92.5% of those with a decline reported non-training stressors, most often work (25.5%), personal life (23.2%) and dieting (22.9%). A greater share of athletes with declines lasting over 4 months reported training to muscle failure (65%).
paper.limitations: Performance decline was self-reported and recalled, so interpretation varies between athletes, and the authors note possible recency bias and that low energy availability may have contributed to some declines. The convenience sample of competitive athletes may not generalize to non-competitive or endurance athletes, repeat entries were not prevented, and the cross-sectional design allows no causal conclusions. Athletes without a decline exited the survey before the training, stressor and symptom questions, so there is no comparison group for how common these stressors or training to failure are in athletes without a decline.
paper.practicalImplications: Fatigue was the most common symptom of an unexplained performance drop, and musculoskeletal aches were common in shorter episodes, so staff can include these in routine checks. Non-training stressors such as work, personal life and dieting were present in most cases, so they should be assessed alongside training load. Because no single symptom predicted overtraining, performance and symptom data should be monitored together.
paper.athleteDev: Athletes who lose performance without a clear cause most often report fatigue, musculoskeletal aches and outside stressors such as work or dieting. Staff can track these alongside performance, but the survey does not show which symptoms predict overtraining.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed competitive resistance-based athletes about unexplained performance declines and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Effects of muscle fatigue on exercise-induced hamstring muscle damage - A three-armed randomized controlled trial.pdf

paper.citation: Schwiete C, Roth C, Skutschik C, Möck S, Rettenmaier L, Happ K, et al. Effects of muscle fatigue on exercise-induced hamstring muscle damage: a three-armed randomized controlled trial. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2023.
paper.abstract: In resistance-trained men, acute or residual muscle fatigue before an eccentric hamstring session did not change most indirect damage markers compared with an unfatigued control group. The acute fatigue group completed less eccentric work during the damage session but showed similar damage. The authors conclude the groups had comparable hamstring damage.
paper.tldr: In resistance-trained men, fatigue before a hard eccentric hamstring session did not increase muscle damage markers compared with no fatigue. The fatigued group that did acute fatigue completed less eccentric work but still showed similar damage.
paper.methods: Three-arm randomized controlled trial with 24 resistance-trained men aged 18 to 35 who trained at least twice a week, randomized by muscle stiffness into an eccentric-only group (ECC), an acute fatigue plus eccentric group (AF/ECC, one 50-rep concentric fatigue set immediately before) and a residual fatigue plus eccentric group (RF/ECC, four fatigue sessions over eight days). The damage protocol was 6 x 10 maximal isokinetic eccentric hamstring curls at 210 degrees per second. Peak torque, muscle thickness and stiffness (shear wave elastography), contractility (tensiomyography), knee range of motion, pain (visual analog scale) and creatine kinase were measured before, after, 1 hour after and at 24, 48 and 72 hours. Mixed-model ANOVA was used.
paper.findings: Eccentric work in the damage session was lower in AF/ECC (6,836 J) than in ECC (9,293 J, P = .005) and RF/ECC (8,654 J, P = .04). Peak torque fell by about 22% in all groups with no group differences, and pain and creatine kinase rose in all groups without group differences. Group x time interactions were found for muscle thickness at BF-mid (P = .02) and for TMG displacement and contraction velocity at BF-distal (both P = .01), but simple between-group comparisons were not significant at any time point; the TMG declines at BF-distal occurred only in the ECC group. Knee range of motion fell in all groups (ECC -21.8, AF/ECC -14.8, RF/ECC -9.4 degrees at 72 h), and stiffness changed over time only at BF-mid in RF/ECC (P = .04).
paper.limitations: Damage was measured with indirect markers, so the study cannot show whether fatigue changes the risk of fibre tears or injury. Residual fatigue was not directly assessed before the damage session, and the residual fatigue group completed its fatigue sessions before the pretest, which the authors note limits interpretation. Groups were small (8 per group), men only, with strict inclusion criteria, and creatine kinase varied widely within groups. The authors' closing Perspective states that acutely fatigued hamstrings show increased susceptibility to damage, which goes beyond the primary result of comparable damage between groups.
paper.practicalImplications: In this trial, a fatiguing set immediately before a hard eccentric hamstring session reduced the eccentric work completed but produced similar damage markers to an unfatigued session. Staff should not assume that less work completed under fatigue means less muscle damage. If TMG or shear wave measures are used to track damage, they should be taken at more than one site, since responses differed within the same muscle.
paper.athleteDev: In resistance-trained men, a fatigued hamstring completed about 26% less eccentric work in the same damage session but showed similar damage markers. Training-load decisions should therefore not rely on work completed alone, and fatigue did not add to eccentric hamstring damage markers in this protocol.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It involved resistance-trained men with experimentally induced muscle damage, excluded acute lower-limb injuries, and measured damage markers rather than injury or rehabilitation outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Getting the most out of intensie longitudinal data - a methodological review of workload-injury studies.pdf

paper.citation: Windt J, Ardern CL, Gabbett TJ, Khan KM, Cook CE, Sporer BC, et al. Getting the most out of intensive longitudinal data: a methodological review of workload-injury studies. BMJ Open. 2018;8:e022626.
paper.abstract: Thirty-four prospective cohort studies of team-sport workload and injury were reviewed for how well their statistical methods fit the repeated, longitudinal nature of the data. Simple methods such as correlations, t-tests and basic regression dominated, while methods suited to repeated measures were rarely used. The authors call for analysis choices that match the theory and the data structure.
paper.tldr: Most team-sport workload-injury studies used simple statistics that do not handle repeated measurements of the same athletes, missing data or the timing of workload. Methods such as mixed models, GEEs and time-to-event models fit this data better but were rarely used.
paper.methods: Systematic methodological review. Six systematic reviews and one consensus statement were searched to identify 34 prospective cohort studies of team-sport athletes with more than 20 workload observations per athlete that examined workload and injury. Two reviewers coded 50 items per study (98% agreement on the first 10 papers). Statistical methods were rated against three theoretical themes (multifactorial aetiology, between- and within-athlete differences, complex systems) and four or more longitudinal design challenges (time-varying and fixed variables, missing data, repeated measures, and time).
paper.findings: Regression was used in 22 of 34 studies, mostly simple logistic regression, and correlation in 10, mostly at team level. Generalised estimating equations appeared in six studies (five logistic, one Poisson), while a Cox model, a multilevel model and a frailty model were each used once. Although 32 studies collected daily workloads, 16 summed them into weekly totals or averages; 23 of 34 did not report how missing data were handled, 20 did not report checking model assumptions, and few included known injury risk factors alongside workload. A rough method score rose to 2.3 for papers since 2016 from 1.6 to 1.9 in earlier periods, and no study analysed the data within a complex-systems framework.
paper.limitations: Only 34 studies were included, found through a search that may have missed some, and the review does not analyse the injury results themselves. The authors note that no universal definition of intensive longitudinal data exists (their cut-off was more than 20 observations) and that study choices were sometimes limited by the equipment, staff or budget available. The method ratings are qualitative and based on how the authors used each tool, not whether it could have been used better. The review is about methods, so it does not estimate injury risk or show whether any workload effect is real.
paper.practicalImplications: When reading workload-injury studies, staff should check whether the analysis handled repeated measurements of the same athletes, missing sessions, and the timing between workload and injury. Simple correlations and team-level weekly averages are weak guides to an individual athlete's injury risk. Analysts working with monitoring data should use mixed or multilevel models or GEEs where they fit the data, and report missing data handling and model checks.
paper.athleteDev: When workload data are used to judge athlete load, weekly totals and team-level correlations can hide day-to-day changes and differences between athletes. Individual analyses that account for repeated measures give a more reliable picture of how workload relates to an athlete's own risk.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It evaluates the statistical methods of workload-injury cohort studies in team sports and gives no guidance on rehabilitation loading or on when an athlete can return.

records.sourceFile: Counteracting mental fatigue for athletes - A systematic review of the interventions.pdf

paper.citation: Sun H, Soh KG, Mohammadi A, Toumi Z, Zhang L, Ding C, et al. Counteracting mental fatigue for athletes: a systematic review of the interventions. BMC Psychology. 2024;12:67.
paper.abstract: Ten randomized controlled trials of interventions to counter mental fatigue in athletes were reviewed. Autonomy support, person-fit, nature exposure, mindfulness and tDCS were each reported to improve some sport-specific performance after a mental fatigue task. Self-regulation and attention resources were proposed as the likely mechanisms, and no meta-analysis was performed.
paper.tldr: Ten small randomized trials suggest that brief mindfulness, autonomy support, short nature exposure and transcranial direct current stimulation may reduce the effects of mental fatigue on sport-specific performance. Each has been tested in only one to five studies, and tDCS showed no benefit in two of its five trials, so these findings are preliminary.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, with searches of Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed and SPORTDiscus up to December 2022 and reference-list searching. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials in athletes that induced mental fatigue with a prior task and compared an intervention to a control on sport-specific motor or perceptual-cognitive outcomes, without supplements. Ten trials were included. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2.0. Results were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity.
paper.findings: Five studies tested tDCS: three reported improved performance after mental fatigue (50 m swim, tethered swimming, basketball decision-making and visuomotor skill), while two found no effect (800 m swim time and basketball shooting accuracy, P = .651). Autonomy support improved tennis serve accuracy (17.10 vs 13.05, P = .04) in one study of 57 semi-professional players, and person-fit comparisons found less performance loss in professional than recreational cyclists and no shooting decline in elite shooters. Virtual nature exposure of 12.5 minutes improved soccer decision-making reaction time (5.01 vs 7.21 s, P < .01) but not accuracy in 90 athletes, and mindfulness improved basketball free-throw accuracy (49.39 vs 40.73, P < .05) in 72 athletes. Physiological indicators and RPE were mostly unchanged, and one study was rated high risk of bias.
paper.limitations: No meta-analysis was done because interventions and outcomes were heterogeneous, and only anodal tDCS could be assessed. The discussion counts four positive tDCS studies, but the results section and Table 2 show no shooting effect in one of them, so only three were positive. Person-fit was a comparison of competitive levels rather than a manipulated intervention, professional athletes were under-represented, only English-language papers were included, and the reported sex split (279 female, 37 male of 316) conflicts with Table 2, which sums to about 253 male and 82 female.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who want to reduce mental fatigue before a skill or decision task could trial brief mindfulness or autonomy-supportive approaches, each supported by one small study, while tDCS evidence is mixed (three of five trials positive). Any approach should be tested against sport-specific performance in the staff's own setting before adoption, since RPE and physiological measures did not change in most studies.
paper.athleteDev: Brief mindfulness, autonomy-supportive decision-making and short nature exposure each improved one sport-specific outcome after a mental fatigue task in a single study. These are candidates to test in training rather than established methods.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It included only athletes without injury and tested performance after an experimental mental fatigue task, with no injured or rehabilitation samples.

records.sourceFile: Dry Needling in Sports and Sport Recovery - A Systematic Review with an Evidence Gap Map.pdf

paper.citation: Kużdżał A, Trybulski R, Muracki J, Klich S, Clemente FM, Kawczyński A. Dry Needling in Sports and Sport Recovery: A Systematic Review with an Evidence Gap Map. Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and evidence gap map of 24 dry needling studies in athletes found that most research concerns pain and recovery. Pain reduction was reported in most studies of injured or pain-affected athletes, while effects on strength, range of motion and performance were inconsistent and limited in healthy athletes. Underrepresented groups include elite, world-class and Paralympic athletes.
paper.tldr: Across 24 studies of athletes, dry needling was most often tested for pain, and several studies found pain relief in injured or sore athletes. It did not reliably improve strength, range of motion or performance in healthy athletes, and safety reporting was incomplete.
paper.methods: PRISMA 2020 systematic review with an evidence gap map, registered on OSF. PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched to January 2024, with reference-list searching. Included studies had athletes at tier two or higher who received dry needling, with healthy or injured athletes eligible, and any randomized, non-randomized or case design. Two reviewers screened and extracted data, and PEDro scores were assigned to 17 experimental studies. Synthesis was narrative with an evidence gap map.
paper.findings: The 24 studies included 580 athletes, mostly tier two (talent or development, 15 studies) or tier three (highly trained or national, 5 studies), with one tier four study and three not classified. Sex was reported as male only in 9 studies, female only in 3, both in 10 and not described in 2. Lower-limb interventions were most common (58.3%). Pain was the most-reported outcome, in 18 studies (75%) by the results section. Of the 17 experimental studies, blinding of participants and therapists was reported in 18%, and allocation concealment in 41%. Only 3 studies reported adverse effects: two local hematomas in one study, mild pain on needle insertion in another, and syncopal responses in two participants plus one episode of chest pain that resolved after medical evaluation in a third.
paper.limitations: The synthesis is narrative, with no meta-analysis, and the 24 studies vary widely in design, dosage and outcome; many of the pain percentages tabulated are within-group pre to post changes rather than differences from a control. Few studies included elite, world-class or Paralympic athletes, no cohort studies were found, dosage and adverse-effect reporting was inconsistent, and blinding and allocation concealment were weak. The review sometimes presents lower pressure pain thresholds after needling as pain relief, and its abstract gives 69% of studies reporting pain outcomes while the results give 18 of 24 (75%); the results figure is used here. The search covered three databases, with eight of the 24 studies found only through reference lists.
paper.practicalImplications: Dry needling may be considered as one option for pain in injured or pain-affected athletes, where several controlled studies reported greater pain reduction than comparison treatments, but dosing was rarely standardized. For healthy athletes, the review does not support using dry needling to improve strength, range of motion or performance. Post-exercise recovery results were mixed, with one study finding cold water immersion better for restoring maximal force, so dry needling should not replace established recovery methods on this evidence.
paper.athleteDev: In healthy athletes, dry needling did not reliably improve strength, range of motion or performance in this review, so it should not be used as a performance enhancer on this evidence. Post-exercise pain results are mixed.
paper.rtp: This review can inform the use of dry needling for pain in injured or pain-affected athletes, where several studies reported pain reduction and some reported better range of motion or balance. It cannot inform return-to-play criteria, since it does not assess injury-specific return timelines, long-term outcomes or the hamstring and other muscles the authors identify as under-studied.
